analysis.one_liner: Funds Washington, D.C.'s government for a year, expands charter schools, and grants legal residency to certain Central American and Caribbean immigrants.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by one vote, 203-202, with every voting Democrat opposed; the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and President Clinton signed it into law on November 19, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the annual spending bill for Washington, D.C., covering schools, police, hospitals, and courts, with about $990 million in federal payments to the city [S5]. Congress used it to attach non-spending rules that override D.C.'s local laws, fund charter schools, and expand management powers over D.C. employees. In the Senate, a plan to limit medical malpractice lawsuits and create private-school vouchers for poor D.C. students was replaced with a law granting permanent residency to certain Nicaraguan, Cuban, Central American, and Eastern European immigrants [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: D.C. residents who rely on public schools, police, fire, hospitals, courts, and homeless services, which receive both federal and local funds [S5]; low-income D.C. families served by newly funded public charter schools [S3][S5]; certain Nicaraguan, Cuban, Salvadoran, Guatemalan, and Eastern European immigrants who gain lawful permanent residence, work authorization, and protection from deportation [S4]; D.C. police officers and firefighters who get five percent raises [S2][S3]; and managed care organizations designated to provide disability compensation services to D.C. employees [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: D.C. service recipients, charter schools, covered immigrants

how_it_helps.text: Provides a $190 million federal contribution to D.C. government operations, with at least $30 million required to repay the city's accumulated deficit, plus federal payments of $169 million for corrections operations, $302 million for correctional facilities construction and repair, and $108 million for the D.C. courts [S5].

Creates the New Charter School Fund, provides $3.376 million for public charter schools and $400,000 for the charter school board, and requires the Mayor to lease unused school buildings to approved charter applicants for one dollar a year [S3][S5].

Under the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act, the Attorney General must grant lawful permanent residence to certain Nicaraguan and Cuban nationals and their families, and sets special rules letting certain Salvadoran, Guatemalan, and Eastern European nationals seek cancellation of removal, with work authorization while applications are pending [S4].

Funds five percent pay raises for D.C. police officers who perform public safety work and for uniformed firefighters, and appropriates money for 12 additional alcohol-beverage inspectors and 10 additional day-care inspectors and monitors [S2][S4][S5].
Requires D.C. to maintain homeless services funding at fiscal 1997 levels [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the roughly $990 million in federal payments to the District [S5]. D.C. government workers bear the risk of layoffs: agency heads may abolish positions and affected employees can be separated without their usual competition or assignment rights [S2][S4][S5]. D.C.'s elected government loses authority, as Congress bars funds for abortion except in cases of life endangerment, rape, or incest, blocks implementation of the district's domestic partners law, caps welfare payment levels the Council may set, and puts the city's finances under closer federal and control-board oversight [S2][S3][S4][S5]. Labor organizations lose a tax exemption on their D.C. real property, and the National Education Association's property is taxed likewise [S3][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, D.C. workers, D.C. self-rule

drawbacks.text: Riders attached to the spending bill override D.C.'s local decisions: funds are barred for abortion except where the mother's life is endangered or in cases of rape or incest, and the city cannot implement or enforce its 1992 Health Care Benefits Expansion Act or any domestic-partner registration system [S2][S4][S5].

D.C. employees in abolished positions can be separated without their normal retention rights, regardless of hiring date, and their disability compensation can only come from Mayor-approved medical officers, hospitals, physicians, or managed care organizations [S2][S4][S5].

Real property of labor organizations in the District, including the National Educational Association's, becomes taxable, and school employee evaluations are made non-negotiable in collective bargaining [S3][S4].

The House-passed version capped medical malpractice noneconomic damages at $250,000, limited punitive damages, and barred punitive damages against FDA-approved drug and device makers, and created private-school scholarships for poor students; both titles were stripped before enactment, so the district's courts and patients saw no change from them [S2][S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The law delivers real money for D.C. services and legal status for thousands of immigrants, which are substantial public benefits. The costs fall on federal taxpayers, on D.C. workers whose layoff protections were stripped, and on D.C.'s limited self-government, since Congress used a must-pass spending bill to override local laws on abortion funding and domestic partners rather than debating those rules on their own merits. The version the House passed by one vote also contained a broad malpractice-limits package favoring physicians and insurers; that package disappeared in the Senate, leaving the enacted law more of a funding-and-immigration measure than the tort and school-choice bill its House title promised.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a single vote along party lines, the Senate amended it by unanimous consent to swap the malpractice and voucher titles for an immigration-relief act, the House accepted the amendment by voice vote, and President Clinton signed it on November 19, 1997 as Public Law 105-100 [S1][S4][S7].

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 203-202 with one member voting present; all 203 votes in favor were Republicans, with 11 Republicans opposed, while 190 of 206 voting Democrats opposed it and none supported it [S7][S8].
A motion by Rep. Jim Moran to send the bill back to committee failed by voice vote before final passage [S7].
The Senate passed the bill with an amendment by unanimous consent on November 9, 1997, and named a conference including Sens. Stevens, Byrd, and Mikulski among others [S7].

The Senate amendment replaced the House's medical liability reform and student scholarship titles with the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act, along with changes such as directing the D.C. Council to set welfare payments comparable to nearby Maryland and Virginia counties and taxing the NEA's D.C. property [S4].

The House agreed to the Senate amendment with an amendment by voice vote on November 12, the Senate accepted on November 13, and the bill was presented to the President on November 17 and signed November 19, 1997 [S4][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Immigrants covered by the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act gained legal status, and charter school operators gained funding and facilities. Physicians, insurers, and voucher advocates lost the malpractice caps and scholarships the House had passed, while congressional Republicans overrode D.C.'s local abortion and domestic-partner policies without the district having any vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: NACARA immigrants, charter schools, congressional Republicans

for.name: Rep. Charles H. Taylor
for.role: House sponsor and Appropriations Committee reporter of the original measure
for.what_they_did: Introduced and reported the original D.C. appropriations bill out of the House Appropriations Committee on October 6, 1997 [S1][S7].

for.name: 203 of 227 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage on October 9, 1997, supplying every vote for the 203-202 margin [S7][S8].

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.what_they_did: Proposed Senate Amendment 1621, which the Senate adopted by unanimous consent, attaching the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act and other changes [S7].

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on November 19, 1997 as Public Law 105-100 [S1][S7].

against.name: 190 of 206 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 190 to 0 among those voting, with no House Democrat supporting the bill [S7][S8].

against.name: Rep. Jim Moran
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back to the Appropriations Committee before final passage; the motion failed by voice vote [S7].

against.name: Rep. Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Moved to reconsider the passage vote, which the House tabled 162-135 [S7][S9].

sides.party_line_note: Final House passage split almost entirely by party: 203 Republicans in favor and 11 against, versus 190 of 206 voting Democrats opposed and none in favor, producing the one-vote margin [S8].

industries.note: The law creates a New Charter School Fund, per-pupil payments, and a revolving loan fund for startup costs, and requires D.C. to lease unused school buildings to charter applicants for one dollar a year [S3][S5]. Parents and students gain alternative public school options while the charter sector's role in D.C. education is locked in [S5].

industries.industry: Managed care organizations serving D.C. workers
industries.note: The law restricts injured D.C. employees' disability compensation to District medical officers and hospitals or Mayor-approved physicians and managed care organizations, removing workers' choice of provider and routing payment through managed care [S4][S5]. Employees lose the option of choosing any Mayor-approved physician or hospital.

industries.industry: Labor organizations, including the National Educational Association
industries.note: The law makes real property of labor organizations in the District taxable like similar organizations, and taxes the NEA's D.C. property specifically, while making school employee evaluations non-negotiable in bargaining [S3][S4].

The House-passed bill would have capped malpractice noneconomic damages at $250,000, limited punitive damages, and shielded FDA-approved drug and device makers from punitive damages, interests that run against injured patients' recovery [S2][S3]. The Senate replaced that title with an immigration law, so none of those protections took effect [S4].
